name: Smart Irrigation System
description: Automate plant watering with a soil moisture sensor, relay, and small water pump when soil gets dry.
guide:
What you will build

A mini irrigation system that turns on a water pump when soil moisture drops below a set level — useful for school gardens and potted plants.

What you will learn

  • How soil moisture sensors report dryness as an analog value
  • How relays switch higher-power devices like pumps
  • How feedback control keeps plants watered automatically
  • How automation supports farming and food security

Safety first

  • Never touch pump wiring while powered
  • Keep electronics away from splashing water — mount the Arduino on a dry shelf
  • Use a low-voltage pump (5–12 V) with teacher approval
  • Disconnect power before changing connections

You did it when…

  • Pump runs when soil is dry and stops when soil is wet
  • You can adjust the moisture threshold in code
  • Water flows through tubing into the plant pot without leaks at joints

Step-by-step instructions

  1. Gather and test the moisture sensor
    Connect sensor VCC to 5 V, GND to GND, and AO (analog out) to A0. Upload a simple analogRead sketch and note values in dry soil vs wet soil.
  2. Wire the relay module
    Connect relay IN to digital pin 7, VCC to 5 V, GND to GND. The relay switches the pump power — do not run pump current through the Arduino pins.
  3. Connect the water pump
    Mount pump in a water reservoir. Attach tubing to the plant. Wire pump positive through the relay COM and NO terminals to the battery or adapter positive; pump negative to supply GND.
  4. Set the moisture threshold
    In dry soil, note analog reading (e.g. 800). In wet soil after watering (e.g. 300). Set THRESHOLD in code between these values.
  5. Upload the irrigation sketch
    Copy the code below. When reading exceeds THRESHOLD (dry), turn relay ON. When soil is moist, turn relay OFF.
  6. Test with a dry pot
    Let a pot dry for a day or use dry soil. Confirm pump activates. Water the soil and confirm pump stops within 30 seconds.
  7. Fix leaks and placement
    Secure tubing with clips. Elevate the reservoir so gravity helps flow. Check no water touches the breadboard.
  8. Record and improve
    Log on/off times for one day. Write one paragraph on how this could help farmers during dry seasons.

Code to upload

Soil moisture pump control (Arduino C)

Adjust DRY_THRESHOLD to match your sensor readings — higher usually means drier on many modules.

const int MOISTURE_PIN = A0;
const int RELAY_PIN = 7;
const int DRY_THRESHOLD = 600;

void setup() {
  pinMode(RELAY_PIN, OUTPUT);
  digitalWrite(RELAY_PIN, LOW);
  Serial.begin(9600);
}

void loop() {
  int moisture = analogRead(MOISTURE_PIN);
  Serial.println(moisture);

  if (moisture > DRY_THRESHOLD) {
    digitalWrite(RELAY_PIN, HIGH);
  } else {
    digitalWrite(RELAY_PIN, LOW);
  }

  delay(1000);
}

equipment.name: Battery pack or adapter for pump

codes.title: Soil moisture pump control
codes.description: Adjust DRY_THRESHOLD using Serial Monitor readings.

name: Motion Detection Alarm
description: Build a room alarm that sounds a buzzer and lights an LED when a PIR sensor detects movement.
guide:
What you will build

A simple security alarm using a passive infrared (PIR) sensor that triggers a buzzer and LED when someone walks into the detection zone.

What you will learn

  • How PIR sensors detect body heat and motion
  • How digital inputs trigger outputs
  • How alarm systems protect homes and schools

Safety first

  • Keep buzzer volume tolerable — do not hold it to your ear
  • Power off before wiring changes

You did it when…

  • Walking past the sensor triggers buzzer and LED within 2 seconds
  • Alarm stops shortly after motion ends (PIR warm-up time allowed)
  • Sensor does not trigger constantly from sunlight on its lens

Step-by-step instructions

  1. Identify PIR pins
    Most modules have VCC, GND, and OUT. Connect VCC to 5 V, GND to GND, OUT to digital pin 2.
  2. Wire the buzzer
    Connect buzzer positive to pin 8 through a 100 Ω resistor (if passive buzzer, use tone()). Connect negative to GND.
  3. Wire the alert LED
    Connect red LED with 220 Ω resistor to pin 9. Cathode to GND.
  4. Wait for PIR warm-up
    After power-on, wait 30–60 seconds before testing. The sensor needs time to calibrate to room temperature.
  5. Upload the alarm sketch
    Use the code below. When pin 2 reads HIGH (motion), turn on LED and sound buzzer.
  6. Test detection zone
    Walk slowly 2–3 m in front of the sensor. Adjust sensor position so it covers a doorway, not a sunny window.
  7. Add a cooldown (extension)
    After alarm triggers, keep buzzer on for 3 seconds then off, even if motion continues — reduces annoyance during testing.

Code to upload

PIR motion alarm (Arduino C)

const int PIR_PIN = 2;
const int LED_PIN = 9;
const int BUZZER_PIN = 8;

void setup() {
  pinMode(PIR_PIN, INPUT);
  pinMode(LED_PIN, OUTPUT);
  pinMode(BUZZER_PIN, OUTPUT);
}

void loop() {
  if (digitalRead(PIR_PIN) == HIGH) {
    digitalWrite(LED_PIN, HIGH);
    tone(BUZZER_PIN, 1000);
    delay(3000);
    noTone(BUZZER_PIN);
    digitalWrite(LED_PIN, LOW);
    delay(2000);
  }
}

codes.title: PIR motion alarm
codes.description: Uses tone() for passive buzzer; use digitalWrite HIGH for active buzzer instead.

name: Obstacle-Avoiding Robot
description: Build a robot car that scans with an ultrasonic sensor on a servo and steers around obstacles on its own.
guide:
What you will build

A small robot that drives forward, measures distance ahead, and turns left or right when an obstacle is closer than 20 cm.

What you will learn

  • How ultrasonic sensors measure distance
  • How servos sweep a sensor left and right
  • How robots make simple navigation decisions

Safety first

  • Disconnect batteries before wiring
  • Keep fingers away from wheels when powered

You did it when…

  • Robot avoids a box placed in its path without being pushed
  • It finds a clear path by looking left and right
  • It recovers after avoiding and continues forward

Step-by-step instructions

  1. Assemble chassis and motors
    Mount two driven wheels and motor driver L298N. Connect motor outputs and battery with teacher help.
  2. Mount ultrasonic sensor on servo
    Fix HC-SR04 on a servo horn so it can pivot. Wire Trig to pin 10, Echo to pin 11, servo signal to pin 9.
  3. Test distance readings
    Upload a test sketch using pulseIn() on Echo. Open Serial Monitor and verify distance changes when you move your hand.
  4. Program scan-left, scan-right logic
    When blocked ahead, stop motors, sweep servo to 45° and 135°, read distances, turn toward the clearer side.
  5. Upload full avoidance code
    Use the sketch below. Tune OBSTACLE_CM and motor speeds on your floor surface.
  6. Course test
    Place two boxes as a gap. Robot should pass through. Widen gap if it gets stuck and retune.
  7. Document decisions
    Draw a flowchart: forward → obstacle? → scan → turn → forward.

Code to upload

Simple obstacle avoider (Arduino C)

Requires NewPing library or basic pulseIn distance function. Tune motor pins to your L298N wiring.

#include <Servo.h>

Servo scanServo;
const int TRIG = 10, ECHO = 11;
const int OBSTACLE_CM = 20;

long readCm() {
  digitalWrite(TRIG, LOW); delayMicroseconds(2);
  digitalWrite(TRIG, HIGH); delayMicroseconds(10);
  digitalWrite(TRIG, LOW);
  long us = pulseIn(ECHO, HIGH, 30000);
  return us / 58;
}

void setup() {
  scanServo.attach(9);
  pinMode(TRIG, OUTPUT);
  pinMode(ECHO, INPUT);
  Serial.begin(9600);
}

void loop() {
  scanServo.write(90);
  delay(300);
  if (readCm() < OBSTACLE_CM) {
    // stop, scan left/right, turn — expand with your motor functions
    Serial.println("Obstacle!");
    delay(500);
  } else {
    // drive forward
    Serial.println("Clear");
  }
  delay(100);
}

codes.title: Simple obstacle avoider (distance test)
codes.description: Start with distance printing; add motor control functions from your line-follower project.

name: Smart Dustbin with Auto-Open Lid
description: Make a touchless bin lid that opens when your hand is detected above the sensor using a servo motor.
guide:
What you will build

A dustbin whose lid opens automatically when you bring your hand within 15 cm of an ultrasonic sensor — no touching required.

What you will learn

  • How distance sensors detect nearby objects
  • How servos create linear lid motion through a lever arm
  • How touchless design improves hygiene

Safety first

  • Keep fingers clear when servo moves
  • Secure dustbin so it does not tip when lid opens

You did it when…

  • Lid opens smoothly when hand approaches and closes after 3 seconds
  • Sensor does not trigger from objects far away
  • Servo mount is firm and does not slip

Step-by-step instructions

  1. Prepare the dustbin
    Choose a light plastic lid. Mark hinge side and mount point for servo arm. Cut a small slot if needed for arm movement.
  2. Mount HC-SR04 above opening
    Fix sensor facing downward over the bin opening. Wire Trig to 10, Echo to 11, VCC 5 V, GND GND.
  3. Attach servo to lid
    Connect servo horn to lid with cardboard lever. At 0° lid closed, at 90° lid open. Test range before gluing permanently.
  4. Upload control sketch
    When distance < 15 cm, move servo to 90°. After 3 s with no hand, return to 0°.
  5. Tune distance threshold
    If lid opens too easily, lower sensitivity (require closer hand). Adjust in code.
  6. Decorate and label
    Add “Smart Bin” label. Explain in your notebook how this reduces germ spread in kitchens and clinics.

Code to upload

Auto-open lid (Arduino C)

#include <Servo.h>
Servo lidServo;
const int TRIG = 10, ECHO = 11;

long readCm() {
  digitalWrite(TRIG, LOW); delayMicroseconds(2);
  digitalWrite(TRIG, HIGH); delayMicroseconds(10);
  digitalWrite(TRIG, LOW);
  return pulseIn(ECHO, HIGH, 30000) / 58;
}

void setup() {
  lidServo.attach(9);
  pinMode(TRIG, OUTPUT);
  pinMode(ECHO, INPUT);
  lidServo.write(0);
}

void loop() {
  if (readCm() < 15 && readCm() > 0) {
    lidServo.write(90);
    delay(3000);
  } else {
    lidServo.write(0);
  }
  delay(200);
}

codes.title: Auto-open lid
codes.description: Adjust servo angles 0/90 to match your lever geometry.

name: Bluetooth-Controlled Robot Car
description: Drive a robot car from your phone over Bluetooth by sending simple letter commands to an HC-05 module.
guide:
What you will build

A two-motor robot car you control with a Bluetooth serial app on your phone: forward, backward, left, right, and stop.

What you will learn

  • How Bluetooth serial replaces a USB cable for wireless control
  • How single-character commands simplify robot programming
  • How wireless links are used in drones and RC vehicles

Safety first

  • Pair and test with car elevated on a box first — wheels off the table
  • Disconnect battery when not in use

You did it when…

  • Phone app connects to HC-05 (LED on module stops blinking when paired)
  • Each command letter moves the car predictably
  • Stop command halts motors immediately

Step-by-step instructions

  1. Wire motors to L298N
    Same as line-follower chassis. Note which pins drive left vs right motors.
  2. Connect HC-05 to Arduino
    HC-05 TX → Arduino pin 10 (RX), HC-05 RX → Arduino pin 11 (TX) through a voltage divider if module is 3.3 V logic. VCC 5 V, GND GND.
  3. Pair phone with HC-05
    Default password often 1234 or 0000. Install a Bluetooth serial terminal app (e.g. Serial Bluetooth Terminal).
  4. Upload Bluetooth drive sketch
    Read Serial on pins 10/11 (SoftwareSerial). Map F/B/L/R/S to motor directions.
  5. Bench test
    With wheels off ground, send each letter and confirm spin direction. Swap motor wires if a side runs backward.
  6. Floor drive test
    Drive in open area. Start with slow PWM speeds (120/255) for control.
  7. Design a simple phone layout
    Write on paper which keys you will press for each move. Optional: use app macro buttons.

Code to upload

HC-05 car control (Arduino C)

#include <SoftwareSerial.h>
SoftwareSerial BT(10, 11);

const int ENA=5, IN1=3, IN2=4, ENB=6, IN3=9, IN4=10;

void motor(int en, int a, int b, int spd, bool fwd) {
  digitalWrite(a, fwd?HIGH:LOW);
  digitalWrite(b, fwd?LOW:HIGH);
  analogWrite(en, spd);
}

void stopAll() {
  motor(ENA,IN1,IN2,0,true);
  motor(ENB,IN3,IN4,0,true);
}

void setup() {
  BT.begin(9600);
  pinMode(IN1,OUTPUT); pinMode(IN2,OUTPUT);
  pinMode(IN3,OUTPUT); pinMode(IN4,OUTPUT);
}

void loop() {
  if (BT.available()) {
    char c = BT.read();
    if (c=='F') { motor(ENA,IN1,IN2,150,true); motor(ENB,IN3,IN4,150,true); }
    else if (c=='B') { motor(ENA,IN1,IN2,150,false); motor(ENB,IN3,IN4,150,false); }
    else if (c=='L') { motor(ENA,IN1,IN2,120,false); motor(ENB,IN3,IN4,120,true); }
    else if (c=='R') { motor(ENA,IN1,IN2,120,true); motor(ENB,IN3,IN4,120,false); }
    else if (c=='S') stopAll();
  }
}

codes.title: HC-05 car control
codes.description: Start with echo test; add motor functions from line-follower project.

name: Foam Glider Design
description: Cut and shape foam gliders with different wing designs, then test which flies farthest and stays stable.
guide:
What you will build

Two or three hand-launched foam gliders with different wing shapes — straight, swept, or delta — to compare flight distance and stability.

What you will learn

  • How wing area and shape affect lift and drag
  • How centre of gravity influences stable flight
  • How to measure and compare experimental results

Safety first

  • Cut away from your body using a craft knife with teacher supervision
  • Launch only in open space, never toward people

You did it when…

  • Each design flies at least 5 m in a smooth glide (not immediate stall)
  • You recorded three flights per design and calculated average distance
  • You explained which wing shape worked best and why

Step-by-step instructions

  1. Draw wing templates
    On foam sheet, draw three wings with equal span (30 cm) but different leading-edge shapes. Label each design.
  2. Cut fuselage and wings
    Cut a 20 cm body strip. Slot the wing through the middle cut. Sand edges lightly for smooth airflow.
  3. Add horizontal stabiliser
    Glue a small rear wing (tail) 5 cm from the back. This keeps the nose from pitching up uncontrollably.
  4. Balance the glider
    Hold at wing root — adjust clay or a paper clip on the nose until it balances near 1/3 back from the leading edge.
  5. Test glide indoors
    Gentle push (not throw). If it stalls (nose up, drops), add nose weight. If it dives, reduce nose weight.
  6. Outdoor distance trials
    Launch from same spot at same angle. Measure landing spot. Repeat 3 times per design.
  7. Report results
    Table of distances, average, and conclusion. Sketch the winning design with force arrows (lift, weight, drag).

name: Kite Building and Flying
description: Build a traditional diamond kite from sticks and plastic, then fly it and observe how wind creates lift.
guide:
What you will build

A classic diamond kite with a cross frame, plastic sail, tail, and bridle string ready to fly on a breezy day.

What you will learn

  • How wind pressure on a tilted surface creates lift
  • How a tail adds stability
  • How bridle position changes flight angle

Safety first

  • Fly far from power lines, roads, and trees
  • Never fly in storms or strong wind above teacher limit
  • Use soft materials — no metal frames that could injure

You did it when…

  • Kite rises steadily in moderate wind and hovers without spinning wildly
  • You can reel in and launch again without tearing the sail
  • You diagram lift and tension forces on the string

Step-by-step instructions

  1. Build the cross frame
    Cross two bamboo sticks: vertical 80 cm, horizontal 60 cm. Tie firmly at centre with string and glue knot.
  2. Notch the ends
    Small notches hold the outline string. Loop string around all four ends to make a diamond outline.
  3. Attach the sail
    Lay plastic over frame, cut with 3 cm margin, fold over string and tape or glue edges tight.
  4. Add tail
    Tie 2 m of ribbon or plastic strips to bottom tip. Tail should be light — add more if kite loops.
  5. Attach bridle
    Tie string from upper third of vertical stick to left and right corners. Flying line attaches to bridle loop.
  6. Test flight
    Partner holds kite downwind. When wind fills sail, release while you walk back slowly. Adjust bridle if kite dives or refuses to rise.
  7. Reflect
    Record wind strength (flags, leaves) and whether tail length helped stability.

name: Python Quiz Game
description: Create a multiple-choice quiz in Python with score tracking and feedback after each answer.
guide:
What you will build

A command-line quiz with at least five questions, four options each, running score, and a final grade message.

What you will learn

  • How to store questions in lists or dictionaries
  • How loops repeat questions until the quiz ends
  • How conditionals check answers and update score

You did it when…

  • All questions display with numbered options
  • Correct and incorrect answers show different feedback
  • Final score prints as X out of Y with a percentage

Step-by-step instructions

  1. Plan five questions
    Choose a topic (science, maths, geography). Write question text, four options, and the correct letter for each.
  2. Create quiz.py
    Store questions in a list of dictionaries: question, options list, answer key.
  3. Loop through questions
    For each item, print the question and options. Ask user to type A, B, C, or D.
  4. Check answers
    Compare input (use .upper()) to correct key. Add 1 to score if correct; else print the right answer.
  5. Show final results
    Print score and percentage. Add messages: 80%+ “Excellent”, 50%+ “Good try”, else “Keep practising”.
  6. Test with a friend
    Let a classmate play. Fix any crashes from empty input or lowercase letters.
  7. Extension
    Shuffle question order using random.shuffle() or add a timer with time module.

Code to upload

STEM quiz game (Python)

questions = [
  {
    'q': 'What gas do plants absorb for photosynthesis?',
    'opts': ['A Oxygen', 'B Nitrogen', 'C Carbon dioxide', 'D Hydrogen'],
    'ans': 'C'
  },
  {
    'q': 'What is the unit of electric current?',
    'opts': ['A Volt', 'B Ampere', 'C Ohm', 'D Watt'],
    'ans': 'C'
  }
]

score = 0
for item in questions:
    print('\n' + item['q'])
    for opt in item['opts']:
        print(opt)
    choice = input('Your answer (A/B/C/D): ').strip().upper()
    if choice == item['ans']:
        print('Correct!')
        score += 1
    else:
        print('Wrong. Answer:', item['ans'])

print(f'\nYou scored {score}/{len(questions)}')

codes.description: Add more question dictionaries to reach at least five.

name: HTML Personal Website
description: Design a multi-section personal website with About, Projects, and Contact pages using HTML and CSS.
guide:
What you will build

A three-page personal website about you: home page with photo and intro, a page listing your interests or STEM projects, and a contact section with your school email.

What you will learn

  • How HTML structure defines headings, paragraphs, links, and images
  • How CSS colours, fonts, and spacing improve readability
  • How navigation links connect multiple pages

You did it when…

  • All three pages link to each other through a menu
  • Site includes at least one image and consistent colours
  • Pages look acceptable on mobile width (text not overflowing)

Step-by-step instructions

  1. Create project folder
    Make a folder my-website with files index.html, about.html, contact.html, and style.css.
  2. Build index.html skeleton
    Add <!DOCTYPE html>, <head> with title and link to style.css, <body> with header nav, main content, footer.
  3. Add navigation menu
    Use <nav> with <a href="index.html">Home</a> etc. Copy the same nav to all pages.
  4. Write About content
    On about.html add your name, class, favourite subjects, and one STEM goal for the year.
  5. Style with CSS
    In style.css set body font-family, background colour, link colours, and max-width on main for readability.
  6. Add an image
    Save a school-safe photo as photo.jpg in the folder. Use <img src="photo.jpg" alt="My photo" width="200">.
  7. Contact page
    Add a mailto link or your school contact info. Do not publish personal phone numbers without permission.
  8. Test in browser
    Open index.html in Chrome/Firefox. Click every link. Resize window narrow to check mobile layout.

Code to upload

index.html starter (HTML)

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8">
  <title>My STEM Portfolio</title>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css">
</head>
<body>
  <nav>
    <a href="index.html">Home</a>
    <a href="about.html">About</a>
    <a href="contact.html">Contact</a>
  </nav>
  <main>
    <h1>Hello, I am [Your Name]</h1>
    <p>Welcome to my STEM portfolio.</p>
  </main>
</body>
</html>

name: Bridge Building Challenge
description: Design and build a popsicle-stick bridge, then test how much weight it holds before breaking.
guide:
What you will build

A bridge spanning 30 cm between two supports, built from popsicle sticks and glue, strong enough to hold at least 1 kg of books or weights.

What you will learn

  • How triangles strengthen structures against bending
  • How to calculate strength-to-weight ratio
  • How engineers test and improve designs

Safety first

  • Wear eye protection when testing to failure — sticks may snap
  • Add weight slowly — do not drop heavy books from height

You did it when…

  • Bridge spans 30 cm and supports at least 1 kg for 10 seconds
  • You recorded mass at failure and calculated bridge mass
  • You identified which joint or member failed first

Step-by-step instructions

  1. Research truss shapes
    Sketch a side view with triangles (Warren or Pratt truss). Label top chord, bottom chord, and diagonals.
  2. Build two side trusses
    Lay sticks on paper over your sketch. Glue joints. Let dry 30 minutes before handling.
  3. Connect with a deck
    Glue cross sticks across the top to join both trusses. Add a flat road deck for loading weights.
  4. Measure bridge mass
    Weigh the finished bridge on a scale (grams). Record in your log.
  5. Set up test supports
    Place two tables 30 cm apart. Bridge ends rest on edges — not glued to tables.
  6. Load gradually
    Center a small container on the deck. Add coins or books one at a time. Note mass when bridge cracks or deflects more than 2 cm.
  7. Calculate efficiency
    Efficiency = mass held ÷ bridge mass. Compare with classmates. Discuss why triangles helped.
  8. Redesign one joint
    Rebuild the weakest joint with overlapping sticks and retest if time allows.

equipment.name: Two tables or chairs as supports

name: Probability Experiments
description: Run coin, dice, and card-draw experiments to compare theoretical and experimental probability.
guide:
What you will build

A data investigation with three mini-experiments: coin flips, dice rolls, and drawing coloured slips — each repeated 50 times with results in a table and bar chart.

What you will learn

  • How theoretical probability predicts long-run outcomes
  • How experimental results approach theory with more trials
  • How to organise data and calculate relative frequency

You did it when…

  • You completed 50 trials for each experiment and recorded outcomes
  • You calculated experimental probability (e.g. 24/50 = 0.48 for heads)
  • You compared to theory (coin heads = 0.5) and explained small differences

Step-by-step instructions

  1. Experiment 1 — Coin
    Flip a fair coin 50 times. Record H or T each flip. Count heads. Experimental P(heads) = heads ÷ 50.
  2. Experiment 2 — Dice
    Roll one die 50 times. Tally counts for faces 1–6 in a table. Which face appeared most? Least?
  3. Experiment 3 — Bag draw
    Put 3 red and 7 blue paper slips in a bag. Draw one, record colour, replace, repeat 50 times. Theoretical P(red) = 3/10 = 0.3.
  4. Draw bar charts
    On graph paper, plot tallies for dice faces or coin H/T. Label axes and title each chart.
  5. Compare theory vs experiment
    Write theoretical values beside experimental ones. Calculate absolute difference.
  6. Discuss sample size
    Would 500 flips be closer to 0.5? Explain in 3–4 sentences using your data as evidence.
  7. Present findings
    One poster or notebook page with tables, charts, and conclusion for the class.

name: Robotic Hand Arm (Manual)
description: Build a cardboard robotic hand with string tendons you pull to flex fingers and pick up light objects.
guide:
What you will build

A life-size cardboard hand with three or four bendable fingers controlled by strings — like tendons pulling when you flex your own fingers.

What you will learn

  • How joints allow rotation in one direction
  • How muscles and tendons work in pairs (flexion)
  • How mechanical design copies biological systems

Safety first

  • Be careful with scissors and needle when threading string
  • Do not snap elastic bands toward faces

You did it when…

  • Pulling a string closes the matching finger smoothly
  • Hand can grasp a ping-pong ball or sponge without dropping immediately
  • You labelled knuckle joints and explained the tendon analogy

Step-by-step instructions

  1. Trace your hand
    On cardboard, trace your hand with fingers spread. Cut out with 5 mm extra width per finger.
  2. Score joint lines
    At each knuckle, score (do not cut through) a line across the finger. This creates a hinge that bends inward only.
  3. Attach straws as guides
    Glue small straw pieces along each finger segment. Thread string through straws from fingertip to wrist.
  4. Secure string at fingertips
    Tie or tape string ends at finger tips. At wrist, leave loose ends to pull.
  5. Test each finger
    Pull one string — only that finger should curl. If others move, separate strings through independent straw paths.
  6. Reinforce palm
    Glue a second cardboard layer on the palm so straws stay attached when pulling hard.
  7. Pick up test object
    Use all strings together to grasp a light ball. Note which finger contributes most.
  8. Write biology link
    Compare your strings to tendons and your scoring lines to finger joints. One paragraph in notebook.
